content.summary_of_the_paper: The manuscript concentrates on Semi-Supervised Semantic Segmentation. The authors notice that the usually adopted training paradigm namely Teacher-Student and consistency training ignores the hardness of samples. To be concrete, perturbation on the hard samples is harmful in training. Moreover, the former works average the losses within batch which ignores the variance for samples. Based on the observations, the manuscript proposes a hardness-adaptive training paradigm, in which a hardness measurement is proposed. Then, samples with different hardness are processed correspondingly, including pertubation and loss evaluation.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
1. The idea is well motivated and the writing is clarified;
2. The proposed Hardness-Adaptive is an efficient pipeline which won' t incur any extra costs, such as data, parameters.
3. The calculation of hardness is reasonable.
4. The experiments are extensive and the results demonstrate the superiority of the proposed method.

Weakness:
1. The idea of treating different samples with theire hardness is not novel at all. The idea is similar with a lot of works, such as Curriculum Learning. What' s worse, as far as I am concerned, there was a paper [1] used the idea of hardness in Semi-Supervised Few Shot Learning. 
2. The idea of measuring the hardness is not novel at all. The hardness measurement is according to the disagreement between two models, which is similar with uncertainty measurement. The uncertainty is to measure the disagreement among multi-models, then the training treats samples with different uncertainty variantly. There were a lot of works adopting similar  ideas, take an example: [2].
3. The idea of making hardness measurement symmetric is not novel, which is similar with JS divergence.
4. The other components used are commonly utilized in Semi-Supervised Semantic Segmentation. 
In summary, the manuscript lacks novelty.

[1] Wang Y, Xu C, Liu C, et al. Instance credibility inference for few-shot learning[C]//Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF conference on computer vision and pattern recognition. 2020: 12836-12845.
[2] Yu L, Wang S, Li X, et al. Uncertainty-aware self-ensembling model for semi-supervised 3D left atrium segmentation[C]//International Conference on Medical Image Computing and Computer-Assisted Intervention. Springer, Cham, 2019: 605-613.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: Clarity, Quality are OK. The authors also submit their code and log files. However, the novelty is the biggest issue.
content.summary_of_the_review: The manuscript has good representation and draft. The whole paper is well organized. As for the idea, I think it is qualified, but not enough to be published on ICLR. Thus, I suggest to reject the submission.

content.title: Response to **Q1: the hardness is not novel.**  and **Q2: measuring the hardness is not novel **
content.comment:
**Q1: the hardness is not novel.** 

Thanks for your comments. As we discussed in related work, exploring hardness is not a new topic. However, our work is different at,

- existing hardness evaluation, either in hardness-related works or curriculum learning, mainly depends on the instantaneous or historical training losses with respect to **ground truths.** In semi-supervised learning, we have no such information. Thus lacking accurate label information makes hardness measurements of unlabeled instances very challenging. Besides, direct utilizing losses (widely adopted strategies) cannot achieve promising results (as shown in Figure 3 a) in the appendix) in segmentation tasks. That is why we carefully design the symmetric class-weighted IOU for hardness evaluations.



- our method are quite different from the work[1] (thanks for sharing this paper). As you mentioned, the so-called credibility in [1] is just like hardness. The paper relies on the evaluated credibility to filter pseudo-labels, a very common technique widely adopted in semi-supervised learning. As we discussed, using the hardness is not new, but the key is how to evaluate accurately and how to leverage this information. [1] relys on an **additional classifier** to estimate the "credibility" while we do not. More importantly, this paper, just like most existing works, utilizes the hardness to select a subset of data, i.e. only requires qualitative results via ranking. Differently, in our work, we need **quantitative results, which** will determine the mixup ratio and trigger probabilities for different instances. In addition, hardness-evaluation for segmentation tasks is more challenging than classification. Straightforward evaluations like losses cannot work well in semi-supervised segmentation.

**Q2: measuring the hardness is not novel**

Thanks for sharing the paper. Similar to question 1, employing hardness/uncertainty/confidence or even attention maps to select reliable pseudo-labels is nothing new in semi-supervised learning. However, almost all existing works just apply some evaluations for selecting /filtering purposes, which only need qualitative results by sorting or setting a threshold. Differently, in addition to our distinct evaluation strategies, we need the quantitative hardness to determine the mixup between strongly and weakly augmented crops, as well as the trigger probability of cutmix. Using losses or prediction flips are not suitable for this semi-supervised segmentation tasks. Thus we carefully explore a symmetric class-weighted IoU in this work.

display_title: Response to **Q3: symmetric measurement is not novel** and **Q4: components used are common**

content.title: Response to **Q3: symmetric measurement is not novel** and **Q4: components used are common**
content.comment:
**Q3: The idea of making hardness measurement symmetric is not novel**

Thanks for the discussion. The symmetric design is everywhere, like in the recent well-known SimSiam. The story is about why we need such a design. Our more challenging quantitative demand needs us to provide a more stable and accurate evaluation than existing hardness-related works. Since there is no ground-truth information and no guarantee that the teacher model consistently outperforms the student, we apply symmetric and class-weighted designs to stabilise the evaluations. Our main contribution is how and why we evaluate the instance hardness in semi-supervised segmentation and how we exploit such information effectively. Unlike recent state-of-the-art semi-supervised segmentation studies, we did not rely on extra network components or additional training losses, but we can still achieve better performance.

**Q4: The other components used are commonly utilized**

Thanks. To the best of our knowledge, there are few works on hardness evaluation for quantitative analysis in Semi-Supervised Semantic Segmentation, and few related works on why and how treating each instance differently can benefit the segmentation performance. In this paper, we did not introduce more advanced operations but leveraged our evaluated instance-level hardness to revise the training loss and to change the augmentation strategies adaptively. Even with these simple modifications, remarkable performance gains can be obtained. 

By the way, in terms of the components, almost all existing studies leverage the mixup and cutmix by using pre-define mixup ratios or trigger probabilities. We relax these things by our evaluated hardness. More importantly, all the operations in our components are closely connected and careful designed. For example, all existing semi-supervised segmentation studies blindly applied various augmentation techniques, but which may hurt the data distribution and over-distort the unlabeled instance. It will signifcantly degrades the final performance, just as discussed in SimpleBaseline[ICCV2021]. We follow this under-explored issue without relying on extra components and alleviate this issue by mixing the strong and weak crops dynamically and adaptively to generate moderate data perturbations. All the adaptive guidance is built upon our hardness evaluations, and, as far as we know, there are no prior studies that extensively designed such guidance in semi-supervised segmentation. Likewise, we carefully revise the unsupervised loss and CutMix augmentation in an adaptive manner. We have discussed more detail and thinkings in our paper. Based on all these designs, despite its simplicity,  our framework can achieve new state-of-the-art performance.

content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper presents a new semi-supervised learning method for semantic segmentation. The most distinctive part of the method is that it measures the hardness scores of training images, which are in turn used to control weights of losses and augmentation strategies for unlabeled images on-the-fly during training. The efficacy of the proposed method on two public benchmarks, where it achieved outstanding performance.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
[Strengths]
- The main idea, measuring the hardness of each training image and adopting loss and augmentation strategy dynamically according to the hardness, sounds reasonable and its effectiveness is demonstrated empirically. 
- The proposed method outperforms latest methods for semi-supervised semantic segmentation by large margins on two public benchmarks. 


[Weaknesses]

I am not fully convinced due to the following two reasons:
- Lack of justification for the underlying assumption: The key idea of this paper is to adapt the loss and augmentation strategy for unlabeled images dynamically during training using their hardness scores, and thus the proposed method depends heavily on the module computing such hardness scores of unlabeled images. The module is based entirely on the assumption that “it is more difficult for the teacher and student models to achieve consensus on a hard example”. Unfortunately, however, the assumption is not verified theoretically or empirically. I personally have no idea why a model and its EMA predict differently for hard examples. 
- Lack of qualitative results: Qualitative analysis of segmentation results is crucial in semantic segmentation studies. However, the paper presents only a few qualitative examples in the appendix. I strongly recommend the authors to add a large volume of qualitative results of the proposed method on both PASCAL and Cityscapes along with comprehensive analysis on the results.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
- Clarity and reproducibility – Good: 

The manuscript is overall written clearly and provides most of the details required to reproduce the reported results. However, I would like to recommend the authors to polish Figure 1, which is currently a bit messy, and to formally define wIOU in page 4. 

- Novelty and quality – Unsatisfactory: 

The key idea of this paper, adapting the loss and augmentation strategy for unlabeled data according to their hardness, is original and has great potential. However, the proposed method is not fully convincing since the underlying assumption for computing such hardness scores is not justified at all. Further, except the hardness computation, the other parts of the proposed method are adopted almost directly from previous work on semi-supervised learning and semantics segmentation.
content.summary_of_the_review: I love the key idea of this paper, appreciate the outstanding performance of the proposed method, and believe it has great potential. However, the distinctive part of the proposed method (i.e., the module adapting the loss and augmentation strategy for unlabeled data according to their hardness) is not fully convincing due to the lack of justification; the other components of the module are simple and rely totally on the estimated hardness. Furthermore, only a few qualitative results are given in the appendix. Hence, I believe the current version of the paper does not meet the standard of ICLR. I would upgrade my rating if the authors well address those two concerns, lack of justification and lack of qualitative analysis.

content.title: Response to Q1
content.comment:
**Q1: the hardness calculations**

Thanks for your suggestions. Here are my explanations. First, accurately evaluating the hardness of unlabeled data is quite challenging. Most related works in hardness-related or curriculum studies require ground-truth information to estimate the hardness. Also, most focus on the classification or detection tasks, and hardness-evaluating on unlabeled samples for segmentation tasks has not been widely explored. A few studies on evaluating unlabeled data just **qualitatively** estimate the hardness and select a subset of unlabeled samples. Nevertheless, in this work, we do need **quantitative** hardness evaluation for following adaptive supervision, which further increases the difficulties.



Second, it is straightforward that, without ground-truth labels, why not use the pseudo-labels from the ensemble model? In many studies, in semi-supervised learning like mean-teacher, self-supervised learning like BYOL, as well as in many self-distillation studies, the EMA model (an ensemble model of historical student models) can be utilized to provide effective supervision. Empirically, an ensemble model can produce better and different predictions. In this job, similar to these studies, we rely on the disagreement between predictions of the ensembling model (**the historical**) and the current student model (**the most recent**) to reflect the instance hardness. High agreements on some unlabeled samples from both models indicate that the model has consistent and confident predictions on these samples throughout many training epochs. Thus, such samples will be regarded as easy samples. As shown in Figure 2 c), we provide numerical hardness evaluations throughout the whole training course. The average and the individual hardness, as well as the standard deviations, gradually decrease as the training processes.



Actually, the predictions between the ensemble teacher model and the most recent student model are quite different, especially at the early training stage. To further improve and stabilize the evaluations, we adopt a symmetric and class-weighted design, as we discussed in the paper.

content.title: Response to Q2
content.comment:
**Q2: Lack of qualitative results**

Thanks. I do understand your concern. I will provide more qualitative results in future revisions. However, regarding the final performance or the overall segmentation results, our method can consistently outperform existing SOTA methods. 


It seems this paper cannot be accepted. I am willing to discuss more BTW. I am not quit enjoying the current research style in semi-supervised semantic segmentation. Since we cannot list all the test images in the paper, only selecting a few of them to provide some insight is not reliable and not convincing enough. As a CV scholar, I prefer comparing the final performance and releasing the source code and training logs for the following studies. Just my personal opinions, and I am expecting yours. 


Besides, integrating more techniques like contrastive learning or ensembling more models to co-training, ... works, certainly, not surprisingly. But it may not contribute a lot to semi-supervised studies. In this work, we hope to drop these additional complicated designs  and return to the clean CR-based semi-supervised framework. (surprisingly, it can work well and achieve new state-of-the-art performance.) We hope this work can inspire future semi-supervised segmentation studies to focus more on semi-supervised issues and explore more model-related dynamic strategies.

content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper tries to solve semi-supervised semantic segmentation (SSSS) from instance differences and training difficulties. Unlike previous works introducing additional training and supervision, this paper proposes HagSeg which uses instance-specific and hardness-adaptive guidance to differentiate unlabeled instances. To evaluate the hardness of unlabeled instances, this paper design a hardness evaluation metric based on model’s performance. The hardness is further used to guide training course on unlabeled data and strong data augmentation on unlabeled instances. The proposed method achieves great improvement over previous methods with a large margin, especially when labeled data is extremely scarce. However, the key role of HagSeg, hardness is unreasonable because of limited theoretical and factual basis. The novelty of HagSeg should be confirmed whether the great improvement comes from hardness guidance or mixed usage of multiple data augmentations.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths
1.	This paper proposes a SSSS method from a novel perspective that tries to differentiate unlabeled data from mining the different importance and training difficulties. With simple but effective hardness metrics and guidance for data augmentation and loss reweighting, HagSeg shows its great performance and potentiality in different SSSS benchmarks.
2.	Compared with the high labeled data situation, we notice that HagSeg shows extremely high performance with scarce labeled data, like 1/16 partition protocol on both classic and blender training sets of Pascal VOC, also in Cityscapes. It is a remarkable method to inspire future works SSSS in an extremely semi-supervised setting.

Weaknesses
1.	Why use wIoU instead of normal IoU when computing hardness in equation 7? And it would be better if providing the definition of wIoU before using it. What’s more, it is more convincible if providing the comparison between using IoU and wIoU.
2.	We notice that your hardness metrics is computed based on IoU between the predictions of teacher and student, which is one metric that reflects the inconsistency between teacher and student. From a consistency regularization view, it represents how CR goes on at current learning steps. Although the ablation study shows the metric value (“hardness”) decreases to a low value as the training procedure goes on, it is not reasonable that this metric evaluates the hardness of unlabeled instances. In my opinion, it is more proper to call it an index representing CR convergence degree instead of hardness. 
3.	In Table.4, the ablation experiment on “Intensity Augs” and “CutMix Augs” shows that it just respectively improves 1.1% and 0.8% with hardness guidance. And in the comparison between the last two control groups (row 8 and 9), the experiment with hardness guidance only improves 1.2% compared with the standard setting, which hasn’t shown great improvement to prove the role of your proposed hardness-adaptive guidance. In other words, we think the mixed usage of different data augmentation is the key role of improvement, which can be observed in row 2 and row 8 in Table.4. The effectiveness of the contributions should be further verified
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: It is an original work, but the effectiveness of the proposed method should be further verified.
content.summary_of_the_review: Please refer to the Strength And Weaknesses.

content.title: Responce to Q1
content.comment:
**Q1: Why use wIoU instead of normal IoU**

Thanks for your comments. Segmentation tasks are very class-imbalanced (background has the largest portion). Directly applying averaging IoU cannot reflect the model performance on different classes, and thus we adopt a class-weighted IoU to address this issue. We expect the evaluation should closely reflect the training status of the model. Besides, the performance using the average IoU cannot obtain promising performance in our method, e.g. on VOC with 1/8 setting, it can only achieve 76.02\%, lower than 77.9\% of using our class-weight designs. As suggested, I will add these details in the future versions.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper1535 by Reviewer Cigi

content.title: Responce to Q2
content.comment:
**Q2: CR convergence**

Thanks for your question! In this work, I use the instantaneous instance "hardness" to estimate 1) the current generalization ability of the mode 2) the current training difficulties of  unlabeled samples. This "hardness" should be closely related to the training status of the model as well as the instance. Personally, the convergence degree is more like a global indicator, but we do need instance-level estimations for following adaptive supervision. With instance-specific and model-related estimations, I can then apply different hardness-adaptive strategies on different instances and at different training stages. I understand your concerns, and I will try to find a better description. Or, any further suggestions?

content.title: Responce to Q3
content.comment:
**Q3: "ablation studies"**

Thanks for the discussion. Here are the explanations. 1) Ablation studies in this setting are not that impressive. As shown in Tab 4, this semi-supervised baseline is already very high 74.7\%. There is no large remaining potential for further improvements. As shown in Tab 1 and Tab 3, our method can significantly improve the segmentation performance in the label-scarce situations and on more challenging Cityscape dataset. I will update this section in the future version. 2) Based on our experimental results, we also found that the augmentation pool used in our intensity-based augmentations also affects the performance a lot. Different from the existing studies in SimpleBasline[ICCV2021] (including 16 different augmentations), we adopt a more moderate intensity-based augmentation pool (12 augs) and a more moderate strength sampling strategy which is beneficial to the final segmentation performance. We did not claim this finding in this paper and adopted a stronger baseline by default (line 8 in Tab4). We will discuss these findings in future works.

content.title: Thank all  reviewers.
content.comment:
We thank all reviewers for their valuable comments. 

In this paper, we aim to highlight the necessity to "treat unlabeled sample discriminatively" and propose a simple yet effective instance-specific and hardness-adaptive algorithm for semi-supervised semantic segmentation. 

We have carefully addressed the main concerns, though the state-of-the-art performance and simple designs may not convince reviewers.  We hope our work can inspire future semi-supervised studies to explore more simple model-related dynamic algorithms to enhance the performance.
